subtopic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
stem:
Write the rate equation for the following reaction:

i. \(\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2}\)

ii. \(2\mathrm{KClO_3} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{O_2}\)
solution:
The rate equation is written by applying the law of mass action.

i. The reactants are \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\)

Rate \(\alpha\ [\mathrm{C}][\mathrm{O_2}]\)

\(\therefore\) Rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{C}][\mathrm{O_2}]\)

ii. The reactant is \(\mathrm{KClO_3}\) and its 2 molecules appear in the balanced equation.

\(\therefore\) Rate \(\alpha\ [\mathrm{KClO_3}]^2\)

\(\therefore\) Rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{KClO_3}]^2\)
_note: p-05 left column, printed p.179. Label printed 'Problem 12.1 :' with a 'Solution :' label.

subtopic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
stem:
\(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)}\)

Write expression for \(K_P\) in terms of \(K_c\).
solution:
\(K_P = \dfrac{(P_{\mathrm{NH_3}})^2}{(P_{\mathrm{N_2}})(P_{\mathrm{H_2}})^3}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NH_3(g)}]^2 [RT]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2(g)}]RT \cdot [\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^3 [RT]^3}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NH_3(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2(g)}][\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^3} \times \dfrac{[RT]^2}{[RT][RT]^3}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C \times RT^{(2-4)}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C \times RT^{-2}\)
_note: p-06 right column, printed p.180. Label printed 'Problem  12.2 :' with a DOUBLE space between the word and the number — one of the label variants the brief warns about.

subtopic: Law of Mass Action and Equilibrium Constant
stem:
Write an expression for \(K_P\) and relate it to \(K_c\) for the following reversible reaction.

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\)
solution:
\(K_P = \dfrac{(P_{\mathrm{HI}})^2}{(P_{\mathrm{H_2}})(P_{\mathrm{I_2}})}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI(g)}]^2 [RT]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}]RT \cdot [\mathrm{I_2(g)}]RT}\)

\(\therefore K_P = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}][\mathrm{I_2(g)}]} \times \dfrac{[RT]^2}{[RT][RT]}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C \times RT^{2-(1+1)}\)

\(\therefore K_P = K_C\)

stem: Write the equilibrium constant expression for the decomposition of baking soda. Deduce the unit of \(K_C\) from the above expression.
_note: p-08 left column, printed p.182. Concentrations of the two pure solids are constant and drop out, per the chapter's own rule in section 12.5.2.

stem: Equal concentrations of hydrogen and iodine are mixed together in a closed container at 700 K and allowed to come to equilibrium. If the concentraion of HI at equilibrium is \(0.85\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), what are the equilibrium concentrations of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2}\) if \(K_C = 54\) at this temperature ?
solution:
Balanced chemical reaction :

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\)

\(\therefore K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI(g)}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}][\mathrm{I_2(g)}]}\)

on substituting the values

\(\therefore 54 = \dfrac{(0.85)^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^2}\)

as initial concentrations of \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2(g)}\) are equal.

(Refer to the balanced chemical equation : 1 mole of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) reacts with 1 mole of \(\mathrm{I_2}\))

Equilibrium concentration of \(\mathrm{I_2(g)}\) = Equilibrium concentration of \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\)

\(\therefore 54 = \dfrac{(0.85)^2}{[\mathrm{H_2(g)}]^2}\)

\(\therefore [\mathrm{H_2(g)}] = 0.12\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

Equilibrium concentrations of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{I_2}\) are equal to \(0.12\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\).
_note: Stem on p-10 left column, solution completes in the p-10 RIGHT column (printed p.184) — the one worked example here that straddles a column break. The book prints 'concentraion' in the stem; transcribed as printed. Arithmetic checked: 0.7225/54 = 0.013380, square root 0.1157, which rounds to the printed 0.12.

stem:
The equilibrium constant \(K_C\) for the reaction of hydrogen with iodine is 54.0 at 700 K.

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{I_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI(g)}\)

\(K_C = 54.0\) at 700 K

a. If \(k_f\) is the rate constant for the formation of HI and \(k_r\) is the rate constant for the decomposition of HI, deduce whether \(k_f\) is larger or smaller than \(k_r\).

b. If the value of \(k_r\) at 700 K is \(1.16 \times 10^{-3}\), what is the \(k_f\) ?
solution:
a. As \(K_C = \dfrac{k_f}{k_r} = 54.0\),

\(k_f\) is greater than \(k_r\) by a factor of 54.0

b. \(K_f = K_C \times k_r = 54.0 \times (1.16 \times 10^{-3})\)

\(= 62.64 \times 10^{-3}\)
_note: p-11 left column, printed p.185. In the printed reaction k_f is set above the forward arrow and k_r below the reverse arrow; those labels are NOT reproduced in the stem because part (a) of the book's own question already defines both constants, so nothing is lost and nothing is added. Publisher-report item (not bracketed, changes no answer): part b prints a CAPITAL 'K_f' where the lowercase rate constant k_f belongs, and gives no unit; 62.64 x 10^-3 is arithmetically correct (54.0 x 1.16e-3 = 0.06264).
